text:
Comments of the State of <u>Washington</u> are generally favorable but the Department of Fisheries feels "loss of management authority in fish and wildlife now vested in the States is clearly a detrimental aspect of the legislation." They recognize provision for delegation of regulatory and management authority to a State and utilization of State facilities and resources in carrying out the endangered species conservation program, but point out there is no mechanism in the bill to fund such activities or programs. The Department of Game says the environmental impact statement does not clearly spell out that jurisdictional responsibilities cannot be sobrogated by the States nor assumed by the Federal Government if the existing balance (of governments?) is to be maintained. The Department of Ecology, while not objecting directly, suggests the role of the States under the Bill should be more fully defined in the EIS. This has been done to the extent appropriate in the "Impacts" section.
The <u>Nevada</u> Department of Fish and Game points out that the proposed legislation tends to usurp the responsibilities of State wildlife agencies.

They feel Nevada has the legal machinery necessary under NRS, Chapters 501-504, even though the State program doesn't take full advantage of it.
The <u>Kansas</u> Forestry, Fish, and Game Commission, objects to tranfer of jurisdiction, from States to Federal agencies, over any resident wildlife species that the Secretary classifies as endangered and calls it "precedent setting."
